title: How the La Brea Tar Pits Work
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Los Angeles (its original Spanish name, pronunciation jokes, Hotlanta) and their visits to LACMA and the Page Museum. They explain the La Brea Tar Pits are asphalt/bitumen seeps from petroleum rising through fissures, how the pits formed during the Pleistocene and the ice age, and why they trap many carnivores. They cover modern finds (cattle, Rodney Dangerfield's reported bones, an LAPD scuba dive), the megafauna recovered (saber-tooth cats, dire wolves, American lions, camels, horses), and the history from Paleo-Indian use and Spanish use, through Hancock family drilling in 1870, William Denton's 1875 fossil description, the 1901 museum digs, the 1913 excavation of 96 pits (Pit 91 especially productive), and Project 23 from 2006, which recovered the Columbian mammoth Zed. They discuss the late Pleistocene extinction hypotheses (human overhunting, climate change, hyperdisease) and the Page Museum's fishbowl lab. The episode closes with a Miracle Mile film mention, promotional plugs, and a listener mail correcting their description of short-term versus working memory.

entities.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art

segments.title: Opening banter on Los Angeles and pronunciations
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Los Angeles' original Spanish name, Hotlanta and Nevada pronunciations, and their visits to LACMA and the Page Museum.

segments.title: What the tar pits are and how they formed
segments.summary: The pits are asphalt or bitumen rather than tar, formed from petroleum seeping through fissures, with some oil evaporating and leaving asphalt. Many millions of years ago the area was underwater; marine life was compressed into petroleum, and the ice age drying led to seeps.

segments.title: Pleistocene animals and carnivores trapped
segments.summary: The pits date to the Pleistocene, and most animals match modern species, which makes the fossils useful for studying past climate. Carnivores are overrepresented because prey and hunting packs got stuck in the tar.

segments.title: Modern trapping, bacteria and recent finds
segments.summary: The pits still bubble and trap animals, including cattle. Methane-producing petroleum-loving bacteria were discovered recently. Hosts mention a reported LAPD scuba dive for evidence in the pits and a claim about Rodney Dangerfield's remains.

segments.title: Megafauna recovered from the pits
segments.summary: Finds include saber-tooth cats, dire wolves, American lions (described as very large), native horses and camels, plus birds and plants. Over 660 species have been found, and the Rancholabrean land mammal age was named for the pits.

segments.title: Early use and Hancock drilling history
segments.summary: Paleo-Indians used the asphalt to waterproof canoes; Spanish settlers used it for roofs and fuel. The Hancock family began drilling for oil in 1870. William Denton described a saber-tooth tooth in 1875, and the natural history museum began digging in 1901.

segments.title: 1913 excavation of 96 pits and Pit 91
segments.summary: Excavators dug 96 pits from 1913, removing mostly large bones and discarding smaller ones, with about four million fossils recovered. Pit 91 was especially productive and was concentrated on for about forty years.

segments.title: Project 23 and the mammoth Zed
segments.summary: Project 23, begun around 2006 to allow an underground parking garage at LACMA, lifted twenty-three large soil blocks in crates. It yielded Zed, the most intact Columbian mammoth skeleton found, displayed in the Page Museum's fishbowl lab.

segments.title: Late Pleistocene extinction hypotheses and human remains
segments.summary: The hosts discuss megafauna die-off in North America and three hypotheses: human overhunting, climate change at the end of the ice age, and hyperdisease. They note the Libreya woman skull, found in 1914, as the only human remains found in the pits.

segments.title: Miracle Mile and film connections
segments.summary: Hosts mention films shot at the tar pits, including Miracle Mile, and talk about actors and a junket they attended.

segments.title: Promotional plugs and show links
segments.summary: The hosts plug their social media accounts, email address, and website.

segments.title: Listener mail on short-term and working memory
segments.summary: A neuroscience PhD student corrects the hosts: short-term memory is no longer used in the field, working memory replaces it, and its capacity depends on item complexity rather than a fixed seven items.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and point listeners to the website for more on the topic.
